entries.original_markdown:
![Figure 3.7 An Ammonium Dichromate Volcano: Change during a Chemical Reaction](/images/section_07/f984737a56da2c1fe4653baf3a49802b.jpg)

The starting material (left) is solid ammonium dichromate. A chemical reaction (right) transforms it to solid chromium(III) oxide, depicted showing a portion of its chained structure, nitrogen gas, and water vapor. (In addition, energy in the form of heat and light is released.) During the reaction, the distribution of atoms changes, but the *number* of atoms of each element does not change. Because the numbers of each type of atom are the same in the reactants and the products, the chemical equation is balanced.

entries.original_markdown:
![Figure 4.4 The Effect of Ions on the Electrical Conductivity of Water](/images/section_08/bc324cdbb2e1ce3fea89e8988424a85c.jpg)

An electrical current will flow and light the bulb only if the solution contains ions. (a) Pure water or an aqueous solution of a nonelectrolyte allows almost no current to flow, and the bulb does not light. (b) A weak electrolyte produces a few ions, allowing some current to flow and the bulb to glow dimly. (c) A strong electrolyte produces many ions, allowing more current to flow and the bulb to shine brightly.

![Figure 23.4 Aqueous Solutions of Vanadium Ions in Oxidation States of +2 to +5](/images/section_27/c21e25a2d4be77abc47e545ccf92446c.jpg)

Because vanadium ions with different oxidation states have different numbers of *d* electrons, aqueous solutions of the ions have different colors: in acid V(V) forms the pale yellow \[VO<sub>2</sub>\]<sup>+</sup> ion; V(IV) is the blue vanadyl ion \[VO\]<sup>2+</sup>; and V(III) and V(II) exist as the hydrated V<sup>3+</sup> (blue-green) and V<sup>2+</sup> (violet) ions, respectively.

From left to right, the solutions contain vanadium in oxidation states +2, +3, +4, and +5. entries.original_markdown:
![Figure 23.5 Compounds of Manganese in Oxidation States +2 to +7](/images/section_27/355ce2892281bd83ab0834a68552d267.jpg)

Like vanadium, compounds of manganese in different oxidation states have different numbers of *d* electrons, which leads to compounds with different colors: the Mn<sup>2+</sup>(aq) ion is pale pink; Mn(OH)<sub>3</sub>, which contains Mn(III), is a dark brown solid; MnO<sub>2</sub>, which contains Mn(IV), is a black solid; and aqueous solutions of Mn(VI) and Mn(VII) contain the green manganate ion \[MnO<sub>4</sub>\]<sup>2−</sup> and the purple permanganate ion \[MnO<sub>4</sub>\]<sup>−</sup>, respectively.
